I. Diwali déjà vu is nice. We are looking forward to the lights and festivities. And Diwali
déjà vu is maddening. In NCR and many other of the country’s urban centres, a large
constituency of unwell citizens and those with children and pets who are scared by
firecrackers or find breathing hard in smoke’s wake, are dreading the onset of bad air. The
apex court itself has been deeply engaged in this conversation for a decade, as have several
govt bodies, civic organisations, business lobbies etc. But here we are yet again, relitigating
the same issues all over again, just as we did last year and the year before that.

Doesn’t the NCR ban on firecrackers hurt the spirit of Diwali? Shouldn’t green firecrackers
at least be permitted? But is there any such thing as a firecracker that’s green? Isn’t it a
false impression being created that these are environmentally safe? But where is the data
showing that it’s the firecrackers that cause the bulk of Diwali pollution? Round and round
we go, as if determined to make no progress whatsoever.

If the stop, start, kneejerk measures are helping, we are not doing any proper measuring of
it. When GRAP restrictions delayed the recarpeting of a Delhi runway last year, we didn’t
tally the emissions of the thousands of waiting and hovering aircraft. BJP to AAP, the past
years have seen different political parties pass the buck, without wholehearted focus on
finding a way out. If NCR is set on a green firecrackers path this Diwali, it will be with the
full foreknowledge that all kinds of pollution will fly through this net. Testing infra is
absurdly inadequate to cover all the points of sale.

The consensus that’s been missing so far is not going to drop down from the smog
tomorrow either. Public policy expert Michael Munger underlines how the adoption of the
US constitution itself defied preexisting rules for consensus, and how lucky this was for
America. He sees the role of constitutions as enabling politics, which in turn is a process
of deciding on rules, such that even the losers accept as legitimate. When the tree-lined
Cheonggyecheon was brought back to life in central Seoul, it meant fighting back
disagreements as much as a vast elevated highway. But it’s a vision that’s paid back South
Korea a million-fold. Restoring India’s rivers, forests, air and soil to health will certainly
not be cost-free. But just as certain is that the costs of failing will be nightmarishly higher.

II. A Child was standing on a street-corner. He leaned with one shoulder against a high
board-fence and swayed the other to and fro, the while kicking carelessly at the gravel.
After a time, a little dark-brown dog came trotting with an intent air down the sidewalk.
A short rope was dragging from his neck. Occasionally, he trod upon the end of it and
stumbled.

He stopped opposite the child, and the two regarded each other. The dog hesitated for a
moment, but presently he made some little advances with his tail. The child put out his
hand and called him. In an apologetic manner the dog came close, and the two had an
interchange of friendly pattings and waggles. The dog became more enthusiastic with each
moment of the interview, until with his gleeful caperings he threatened to overturn the
child. Whereupon the child lifted his hand and struck the dog a blow upon the head.

This thing seemed to overpower and astonish the little dark-brown dog, and wounded him
to the heart. He sank down in despair at the child's feet. When the blow was repeated,
together with an admonition in childish sentences, he turned over upon his back, and held
his paws in a peculiar manner. At the same time with his ears and his eyes he offered a
small prayer to the child.

Presently he struggled to his feet and started after the child. He looked so comical on his
back, and holding his paws peculiarly, that the child was greatly amused and gave him little
taps repeatedly, to keep him so. But the little dark-brown dog took this chastisement in the
most serious way, and no doubt considered that he had committed some grave crime, for
he wriggled contritely and showed his repentance in every way that was in his power. He
pleaded with the child and petitioned him, and offered more prayers.

At last the child grew weary of this amusement and turned toward home. The dog was
praying at the time. He lay on his back and turned his eyes upon the retreating form.
Presently he struggled to his feet and started after the child. The latter wandered in a
perfunctory way toward his home, stopping at times to investigate various matters. During
one of these pauses he discovered the little dark-brown dog who was following him with
the air of a footpad.

On the way to his home the child turned many times and beat the dog, proclaiming with
childish gestures that he held him in contempt as an unimportant dog, with no value save
for a moment. For being this quality of animal the dog apologized and eloquently expressed
regret, but he continued stealthily to follow the child. His manner grew so very guilty that
he slunk like an assassin.

between past, present, and future begins to blur. Some physicists now suggest that all

IV. There is an understandable, if sometimes counterproductive, tendency in New Delhi to
view Pakistan’s internal tensions and contradictions only through the prism of a fraught
bilateral relationship. The recent clash between Pakistani and Afghan forces during
Afghanistan’s Foreign Minister and Taliban leader Amir Khan Muttaqi’s visit to India, and
its fallout, is a case in point. This round of violence began with Pakistan’s airstrikes inside
Afghan territory, followed by Kabul’s retaliation through the capture of military posts
across the Durand Line. Security personnel have died on both sides. The state of ties
between Rawalpindi and Kabul is clearly of strategic significance to India and the wider
region. It is equally important, however, to understand the deeper historical and cultural
roots of this conflict, and to assess whether Pakistan’s leadership is capable of drawing the
right lessons.
In August 2021, when the U.S. withdrew from Afghanistan after two decades, Islamabad
barely concealed its jubilation. It saw the Taliban’s return as another opportunity to chase
the chimaera of “strategic depth”. That triumphalism was short-lived. Long-standing
issues between the two countries, dating back to Partition, remained unresolved. Kabul
does not recognise the Durand Line, and Pakistani fears of “Pashtunistan” still shape its


frontier policy. Islamabad and Rawalpindi accuse the Taliban of sheltering the Tehreek-e-
Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and other militants who strike across the border. Simultaneously,
the Pakistan army and government have dismissed bodies such as the Pashtun Tahafuz
(self-respect) Movement, a peaceful platform seeking dialogue on rights and autonomy.
Kabul, for its part, has long resented being treated as a puppet by Rawalpindi.
The people of Pakistan, and others in the region who have suffered from the adventurism
of its military-intelligence establishment, remain the victims of a cruel irony. Pakistan’s
own policies have tied Islamabad’s hands, and violence has become a normal instrument
of politics: protests against Israel by the fundamentalist Tehreek-e-Labbaik Pakistan (TLP)
have also turned violent and invited crackdowns. The use of religion and fundamentalist
non-state actors for strategic ends can have no happy ending. India will watch closely how
Pakistan’s government and army handle domestic discontent and external challenges. An
unstable Pakistan bodes ill for regional security.

V. For most of India's vehicle owners, norms are mere suggestion, and adherence optional.
Of the 407 mn registered vehicles, nearly 325 mn (70%) don't have one or more of the
mandatory pollution and general fitness certificates and insurance. 2-wheelers, the gateway
vehicle, are the biggest offenders - there are 235 mn of them that are non-compliant. This
leaves just 82 mn fully-compliant rule-following vehicles. This disregard gives a sense of
the civic sense of Indians. But if the individual has been less than a stellar citizen, the state,
too, has failed - unable to create awareness and turning a blind eye to systemic non-
compliance.

Attitude to compliance is indicative of whether a country can ever be 'developed' or not.
Norm-based society forms the core of a developed country. Norms are not suggestions, but
understood as rules that underpin orderly functioning of a society, balancing individual
freedoms with duties, safety, comfort. Non-compliance comes with a high price tag.
Developing countries like ours are not lacking in norms. Cost of non-compliance - on paper
- is not low. The big gap is implementation. Raising the actual cost of non-compliance -
not just imposing higher fines but loss of licence, and filing FIRs (as Delhi Police has now
implemented for driving on the wrong side of the road) - is the right way forward.

That the government is reportedly prepared to take measures to ensure that all vehicles
meet regulatory norms is a good step. However, it must find workable ways to make
people understand that norms and regulations on Indian roads are not just for show and
theoretical niceties. The stick of disincentives must go hand in hand with the carrot of


awareness if India has any intention of becoming viksit - beyond theory.

V. For most of India's vehicle owners, norms are mere suggestion, and adherence optional.
Of the 407 mn registered vehicles, nearly 325 mn (70%) don't have one or more of the
mandatory pollution and general fitness certificates and insurance. 2-wheelers, the gateway
vehicle, are the biggest offenders - there are 235 mn of them that are non-compliant. This
leaves just 82 mn fully-compliant rule-following vehicles. This disregard gives a sense of
the civic sense of Indians. But if the individual has been less than a stellar citizen, the state,
too, has failed - unable to create awareness and turning a blind eye to systemic non-
compliance.

Attitude to compliance is indicative of whether a country can ever be 'developed' or not.
Norm-based society forms the core of a developed country. Norms are not suggestions, but
understood as rules that underpin orderly functioning of a society, balancing individual
freedoms with duties, safety, comfort. Non-compliance comes with a high price tag.
Developing countries like ours are not lacking in norms. Cost of non-compliance - on paper
- is not low. The big gap is implementation. Raising the actual cost of non-compliance -
not just imposing higher fines but loss of licence, and filing FIRs (as Delhi Police has now
implemented for driving on the wrong side of the road) - is the right way forward.

That the government is reportedly prepared to take measures to ensure that all vehicles
meet regulatory norms is a good step. However, it must find workable ways to make
people understand that norms and regulations on Indian roads are not just for show and
theoretical niceties. The stick of disincentives must go hand in hand with the carrot of


awareness if India has any intention of becoming viksit - beyond theory.

questions.stimulus:
X. In contract law, the formation of a valid agreement depends fundamentally on the
presence of an offer and its acceptance. An offer is a clear expression of willingness by one
party, the offeror, to enter into a legally binding relationship on definite terms, with the
intention that it shall become binding as soon as it is accepted by the other party. An offer


must be distinguished from a mere invitation to offer. Advertisements, price lists, and
display of goods generally indicate an intention to invite offers, not to make binding
promises, unless the language shows a clear commitment. Acceptance is the unqualified
and absolute assent to the terms of the offer. For acceptance to be valid, it must correspond
exactly with the offer and must be communicated to the offeror, unless the offeror has
waived the requirement of communication. Silence, as a general rule, does not amount to
acceptance. Acceptance may be expressed in words or implied through conduct, such as
performing the conditions of the offer. The timing of acceptance is also significant. An
offer can be revoked at any time before acceptance is complete against the offeror. Once
acceptance is validly communicated, a binding contract comes into existence, and neither
party can unilaterally withdraw. In cases of communication by post, acceptance is complete
against the offeror when it is properly posted, even if it is delayed or lost, reflecting the
“postal rule.” However, acceptance must be given while the offer is still in force. An offer
may lapse after a reasonable time, on rejection, on the death of the offeror, or if a condition
attached to the offer is not fulfilled. The law of offer and acceptance thus ensures certainty
by clearly identifying when negotiations end and contractual obligations begin.

questions.stimulus:
XI. Equality is a foundational value of constitutional democracies, yet its meaning is often
misunderstood. Two dominant conceptions of equality in legal theory are formal equality
and substantive equality. Formal equality is grounded in the idea that “likes should be
treated alike.” Under this approach, the law must apply uniformly to all persons, without
distinction. If a rule is neutral on its face and applies equally to everyone, formal equality
considers it fair, even if its effects are unequal. This conception prioritises sameness and
non-discrimination in form. Substantive equality, by contrast, focuses on outcomes rather
than appearances. It recognises that individuals and groups do not start from the same
social, economic, or historical position. Treating unequal persons identically may
perpetuate, rather than reduce, disadvantage. Substantive equality, therefore, permits, and
sometimes requires, differential treatment to achieve genuine equality. Measures such as
reservations, affirmative action, or targeted welfare schemes are justified under this
approach because they seek to correct structural barriers faced by disadvantaged groups.
Constitutional courts have increasingly moved beyond a purely formal understanding of
equality. In India, Article 14 has been interpreted not merely as a guarantee against
arbitrary classification, but as a tool to achieve real equality. This shift explains why laws
that treat people differently are not automatically unconstitutional; the key question is
whether the differentiation is aimed at reducing disadvantage or reinforcing it. A law that
appears neutral may still violate equality if it disproportionately harms a vulnerable group,
while a law that explicitly distinguishes between groups may be upheld if it promotes
fairness in substance. However, substantive equality is not limitless. Differential treatment
must have a rational connection to the goal of equality and must not create new forms of
exclusion or stigma. The challenge for courts lies in balancing uniformity with
responsiveness, ensuring that equality is not reduced to mechanical sameness, nor distorted
into unchecked preference. Ultimately, equality in law is not merely about equal rules, but
about equal concern and respect.

equality/, 31-03-2025

questions.stimulus:
XII. Medical negligence law in India has undergone significant development as courts
increasingly recognise the right to health and medical treatment as an integral component
of the right to life under Article 21 of the Constitution. Traditionally, claims of medical
negligence were assessed through the lens of tort law, requiring the patient to establish
duty of care, breach, and resultant harm. However, recent judicial trends have expanded
the scope of state and institutional responsibility, especially in cases involving denial of
treatment or emergency care. Courts have repeatedly held that government hospitals and
public health authorities cannot refuse treatment on the grounds of administrative
constraints, lack of infrastructure, or non-availability of beds when a patient’s life is at
stake. The obligation to provide timely medical assistance arises not merely from
contractual relationships but from constitutional duty. Even private hospitals, once they
undertake treatment, are expected to adhere to reasonable standards of care and cannot
arbitrarily withdraw services in emergency situations. Importantly, courts distinguish
between medical negligence and medical error. An error of judgment does not
automatically amount to negligence unless it falls below the standard of care expected
from a reasonably competent medical professional. At the same time, systemic failures,
such as the absence of oxygen supply, delay in ambulance services, or refusal to admit
critically ill patients, are increasingly treated as violations of the right to treatment rather
than isolated acts of negligence. Another evolving aspect is the recognition that the right
to treatment includes access to emergency care without preconditions such as advance
payment or documentation. Judicial pronouncements emphasise that procedural
formalities cannot override the urgency of saving human life. Compensation in such
cases is not merely corrective but also serves a deterrent purpose, signalling that health
governance must prioritise patient welfare over institutional convenience. Thus,
contemporary medical negligence jurisprudence reflects a shift from individual fault-

attract constitutional scrutiny.

XIII. In criminal law, liability is traditionally founded on the coexistence of two core
elements: actus reus and mens rea. Actus reus refers to the external conduct of the accused,
the physical act or omission that the law prohibits. Mens rea represents the mental element
accompanying the act, such as intention, knowledge, recklessness, or negligence. The
classical principle governing criminal responsibility is captured in the maxim actus non
facit reum nisi mens sit rea, meaning that the act alone does not make a person guilty unless
the mind is also blameworthy. Ordinarily, both elements must be present at the same time.
A guilty intention formed after the completion of an act does not create criminal liability,
just as a mere intention without any corresponding conduct does not attract punishment.
This requirement reflects the law’s concern with moral culpability rather than mere harmful
outcomes. However, this principle admits important exceptions. Certain offences, known
as strict liability offences, do not require proof of mens rea. In such cases, the commission
of the prohibited act itself is sufficient for liability. These offences are commonly found in
regulatory statutes dealing with public health, safety, and welfare, where proving intention
would be impractical and enforcement would suffer. Here, the law prioritises prevention
over blame. Criminal liability may also arise from omissions, but only where there exists
a legal duty to act. Failure to perform a moral duty alone does not amount to an offence;
the duty must be imposed by law. For example, a guardian may be criminally liable for


failing to protect a child if such omission leads to harm. Thus, criminal law carefully
balances the requirement of a guilty mind with practical considerations of social protection,
ensuring that liability is imposed only when justified by law.

questions.stimulus:
XV. In public law and regulatory governance, delegated legislation plays a crucial role in
implementing statutory objectives while balancing administrative efficiency and
democratic accountability. Legislatures often enact broad framework statutes and delegate
rule-making powers to the executive or specialised authorities to fill in operational details.
Such delegation is considered necessary in modern governance, given the technical
complexity and evolving nature of regulation. However, this delegation is not unlimited. A
fundamental constitutional principle governing delegated legislation is that essential
legislative functions cannot be delegated. The legislature must lay down the policy,
purpose, and guiding principles of the law. Delegated authorities may only determine
details, procedures, or technical standards within this framework. If the parent statute
confers unfettered discretion without clear guidance, the delegation may be struck down
as excessive or unconstitutional. Judicial review of delegated legislation primarily focuses
on ultra vires control. A rule or regulation may be invalidated if it exceeds the scope of
authority granted by the parent statute, contradicts the statute’s objectives, or violates
constitutional provisions. Courts also examine whether delegated legislation is arbitrary,
unreasonable, or manifestly unjust, especially when it affects fundamental rights or
imposes penalties. At the same time, courts recognise that delegated legislation enjoys a
presumption of validity. Judicial intervention is cautious, particularly in areas involving
technical expertise, economic regulation, or public welfare. The role of the court is not to
assess the wisdom of the rule but to ensure that it remains within legal boundaries. Thus,


delegated legislation reflects a delicate balance: it enables flexible and responsive
governance, yet remains constrained by constitutional limits, legislative intent, and the
principles of accountability and rule of law.

questions.stimulus:
XVII. What is the self? The human condition is defined by our awareness that we are
distinct from the world, that we are, in some way, the same person from day to day, even
though our bodies change, and that the people around us are also selves. But we still do
not really know what we are. As William James explained more than a century ago, the
dual nature of the self lies at the heart of the mystery – the self is this most unusual thing,
in that it is both the perceiver of itself and the content of what it perceives. Right now, for
instance, ‘I’ can sense ‘my’ fingers as they type. I can also see a screen on which my words
appear, and, if I choose, I can focus instead on the rims of my glasses, which move as my
head moves. Interestingly, ‘my’ can refer not just to body parts but to things I wear, think
or do. Although the skin is an important boundary between self and not-self, the self is
more than just the physical body – it is also a set of ideas about who and what I am.

With the advent of generative artificial intelligence (genAI) that can converse fluidly in the
first person, people are asking whether such AIs might someday have a sense of self.
Indeed, might they have one already? (OpenAI’s GPT-5, perhaps reassuringly, says it does
not.) This question is hard to answer for several reasons, but particularly because we still
lack a good understanding of the human self. Significant progress is being made, however,
through philosophical, psychological and neuroscientific investigations, and most recently
by an approach that I and others have been exploring – the attempt to create or synthesise
a sense of self in robots.

Based on what we have learned, I believe a foundational aspect of the human self is that
we have physical bodies, and that our experience emerges from a fundamental distinction
between what is, and what is not, a part of the ‘embodied’ me. If this is true, then a
disembodied AI could never have a sense of self similar to our own. However, for robots
that inhabit our physical world through a body – even one quite different to our own – the
bets may be off.


[Extracted with revisions and edits from “The synthetic self”, aeon.]

questions.stimulus:
XX. India’s mergers and acquisitions market is getting bigger, but quieter. Deal values hit
$14 billion in Q3 2025, up 50 per cent from the year before. Yet, fewer deals are closing.
Companies are doing larger but fewer transactions, and smaller deals are falling away.

Mergers are important because they offer real exits to shareholders, and enable firms to
grow bigger, allowing them to optimize economies of scale and create surplus for
consumers. For a government that wants to focus on ease of doing business and has
aspirations of a $7.3 trillion economy, months lost in tribunal queues carry a real cost to
shareholders and Indian firms wanting to grow.

In her Union Budget 2025 speech, finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman offered a
diagnosis. Requirements and procedures for speedy approval of company mergers were to
be rationalised, and the scope for fast-track mergers widened. In September, the Ministry


of Corporate Affairs followed through. The Companies (Compromises, Arrangements and
Amalgamations) Amendment Rules, 2025 expanded the fast-track merger framework,
allowing unlisted companies with borrowings under Rs 200 crore, holding-subsidiary
mergers, and fellow subsidiary restructurings to bypass the tribunal entirely, getting
approval directly from the Regional Director.

It was an acknowledgement that the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), the single
window meant to speed up corporate restructuring, has become a bottleneck. At The
Professeer, we analysed 3,376 merger cases filed after 2021 across all benches to
understand exactly where deals go to wait. These cases account for a fifth of the caseload
of the tribunal today.

On paper, a merger through NCLT should take 90-120 days. First, the company files an
application. Let’s call it the First Motion, the green light to talk to stakeholders. The
tribunal decides whether shareholders and creditors need to formally vote, or if that
requirement can be waived. Then comes a 30-day window for regulators – the Regional
Director, Income Tax, Registrar of Companies, and others – to raise objections. Finally, the
company files a Second Motion, and the NCLT approves or rejects the scheme. This
approval may be conditional or unconditional.

[Extracted with revisions and edits from “NCLT bottleneck hinders India’s M&A boom.
Govt’s fast-track framework ignores the real problem”, ThePrint.]

questions.stimulus:
XX. India’s mergers and acquisitions market is getting bigger, but quieter. Deal values hit
$14 billion in Q3 2025, up 50 per cent from the year before. Yet, fewer deals are closing.
Companies are doing larger but fewer transactions, and smaller deals are falling away.

Mergers are important because they offer real exits to shareholders, and enable firms to
grow bigger, allowing them to optimize economies of scale and create surplus for
consumers. For a government that wants to focus on ease of doing business and has
aspirations of a $7.3 trillion economy, months lost in tribunal queues carry a real cost to
shareholders and Indian firms wanting to grow.

In her Union Budget 2025 speech, finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman offered a
diagnosis. Requirements and procedures for speedy approval of company mergers were to
be rationalised, and the scope for fast-track mergers widened. In September, the Ministry


of Corporate Affairs followed through. The Companies (Compromises, Arrangements and
Amalgamations) Amendment Rules, 2025 expanded the fast-track merger framework,
allowing unlisted companies with borrowings under Rs 200 crore, holding-subsidiary
mergers, and fellow subsidiary restructurings to bypass the tribunal entirely, getting
approval directly from the Regional Director.

It was an acknowledgement that the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), the single
window meant to speed up corporate restructuring, has become a bottleneck. At The
Professeer, we analysed 3,376 merger cases filed after 2021 across all benches to
understand exactly where deals go to wait. These cases account for a fifth of the caseload
of the tribunal today.

On paper, a merger through NCLT should take 90-120 days. First, the company files an
application. Let’s call it the First Motion, the green light to talk to stakeholders. The
tribunal decides whether shareholders and creditors need to formally vote, or if that
requirement can be waived. Then comes a 30-day window for regulators – the Regional
Director, Income Tax, Registrar of Companies, and others – to raise objections. Finally, the
company files a Second Motion, and the NCLT approves or rejects the scheme. This
approval may be conditional or unconditional.

[Extracted with revisions and edits from “NCLT bottleneck hinders India’s M&A boom.
Govt’s fast-track framework ignores the real problem”, ThePrint.]
